chunks: And it was narrated from Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad al-Hamadhānī, who said:

I wrote to Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام: A man wrote a document in his own handwriting, but he did not say to his heirs, "This is my will," nor did he say, "I have made a bequest." Rather, he only wrote a document containing what he wished to bequeath. Is it obligatory upon his heirs to carry out what is in the document in his handwriting, even though he did not command them to do so?
So he عليه السلام wrote: "If he has children, they are to carry out everything they find in their father's document, whether in the way of righteousness or otherwise."

key_terms.أَوْصَيْتُ: I made a bequest or will
key_terms.الْقِيَامُ بِمَا فِي الْكِتَابِ: carrying out what is written in the document
key_terms.فِي وَجْهِ الْبِرِّ: in the direction of righteousness; acts of goodness
key_terms.وَرَثَتِهِ: his heirs; those who inherit from the deceased
key_terms.وَصِيَّتِي: my will; a formal testamentary bequest

ai.seo_question: Is a handwritten will binding in Islam if the deceased did not explicitly tell his heirs that it was his وصيّة?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling concerning a written bequest that was not verbally declared as a وصيّة. It indicates that when children find their father's written instructions, they are to carry out what is recorded therein. The narration is relevant to the fiqh of wills, inheritance, and the authority of written testamentary documents.
